chapter: Returning to the US and the Savoy band
title: Running the band alone: agents and no financial backing
summary: His Savoy band toured and returned but folded; unlike many big bands he had no backer and handled everything himself.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: So you stayed several months at the Savoy and -- did you tour again with that band after this early 1939 engagement at the Savoy?
Yes, we went, you know, out and back in to the Savoy, and you know, a couple of times. Yes.
And then that band -- you had to let go, as time went on similarly to the previous occasion.
That's right. Not enough work to keep everyone together.
And do you feel -- at the time, or do you feel now, that if you had had -- did you have a regular booking agent for the band?

Yes, we had a couple of agents. We had the Gayle Agency for awhile, and we had the Joe Glaser Agency for awhile, and I don't know ... I guess I could never make the proper kind of deals with agents that they wanted.

Uh huh. Did some of these big bands at that time -- a lot of them were springing up of course -- after, you know, at the height of the Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller, Harry James, Gene Krupa, you know, everybody was coming out of the bands and forming their own band -- and so did those bands have, so far as you know, big backing -- financial backing?
Well, many of them did. They had to have. Yeah.
Yeah. But you didn't have that kind of backer?
No, not at all.
Nothing at all then?
Nothing at all, no.
You had to run the whole thing yourself, actually -- you had to be the main booker, the arranger, the leader, the soloist, and all these things?
Band boy ...
The band boy, too.
No, I had no financial assistance.

Well, maybe if you had had that kind of backing, and had been able to concentrate on the musical side of the whole band and you had reasonable booking arrangements, that you could have kept the band longer, and it would have become something more of a familiar landmark, not only to jazz historians and critics, but also to the public at large. But you don't want to think about that.

Well, no. I think you're right. That's a good observation, and I agree. I think so. I think that something much more could have happened had there been someone sufficiently interested enough, to say, 'Well, gee, this thing deserves financing and maybe I can make some money out of it,' you know.
Yeah. It seems that you could never keep them together long enough to have them take with the public.
That's right.
